prose.en: Many words in English function as noun and verb, or verb and adjective, or noun and adjective, with the same form.
What's the answer? (noun) I must clean my room. (verb) I don't like the cold. (noun) Answer the question. (verb) It's a clean room. (adj) I don't like cold weather. (adj)
The same word form can have different meanings, but this unit looks at examples where the meaning is the same or similar, and concentrates on nouns and verbs with the same form.

brake (= stop a car using the brake on the floor) ring (= telephone) diet (= eat less to lose weight) queue (= wait in a line of people) guess (= give an answer without knowing the facts) murder (= kill someone)

Many common words can function as noun and verb with the same form and meaning: drink, rest, look, cost, swim, wash, push, pull, reply, kiss, chat (= a casual conversation infml) [also practise (v) and practice (n)].
It is often more natural in English to use the verb + noun structure (e.g. had a guess) and not the verb (e.g. guessed). You need to know which verbs to use with the nouns.

verb: I didn't know the answer, so I guessed. We rested for a while. She braked suddenly. He needs to diet. I'm going to ring him. I looked in the paper. I dreamt about you last night. We had to queue for half an hour.

verb + noun: I didn't know the answer, so I had a guess. We had a short rest. She put on the brakes suddenly. He needs to go on a diet. I'm going to give him a ring. I had a look in the paper. I had a dream about you last night. We had to wait in a queue for half an hour.
